The White-winged nightjar (Eleothreptus candicans) is a cryptic, insectivorous bird inhabiting the cerrado savannas of central South America. Newly hatched chicks, which emerge from eggs incubated under a tightly regulated thermal regime of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], display a markedly altricial condition, with their eyes closed and sparsely covered in down. The age at which hatching occurs is approximately 19 days [ab = approximately 19 days] under these conditions, a value consistent with that observed during artificial incubation protocols used for several capri at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]mulgid species. Upon emergence, the wet weight of a neonate is remarkably low, averaging a mere 5.5 grams [Wwb = 5.5 grams]; this modest mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the embryo and the heavy reliance on immediate parental provisioning. The energetic demands of rapid somatic growth require the brooding adult to maintain a stable nest microclimate, and it is notable that the development of the altricial nestling proceeds at a pace that ultimately yields a fully grown adult with an ultimate wet weight of 46 grams [Wwi = 46 grams]. This nearly tenfold increase in mass from hatching to adulthood is a testament to the intensive feeding effort by both parents, which must deliver a steady supply of flying insects to the hungry chick.

Under the standard metabolic conditions typical of active adult caprimulgids, which operate at a body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], several key developmental milestones are attained by growing nestlings. The first major threshold is the fledging event, when the young bird achieves sustained flight for the first time, which occurs at 19.5 days after hatching [tx = 19.5 days after hatching] under these thermal conditions at a temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C]. This relatively short nestling period is characteristic of the family and allows the fledgling to leave the vulnerable ground nest and begin exploring the surrounding habitat, although it remains dependent on its parents for food for some weeks afterward. The fledgling precursor, having completed the growth of its primary flight feathers, then enters a juvenile phase where it continues to refine its foraging skills. The transition from a sedentary nestling to a mobile fledgling is thus a critical period in the life cycle, and the specific timing of this event is tightly linked to the ambient thermal environment, which influences both metabolic rate and the rate of muscle and feather development in the pin-feathered chick.

Following the fledging milestone, the immature bird undergoes a prolonged period of somatic growth and behavioral maturation before reaching reproductive competence. Continuing under the same thermal regime of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], the age at which the gonads become fully functional and the bird reaches puberty is documented at 58.5 days after hatching [tp = 58.5 days after hatching]. This marks the point at which the juvenile bird transitions from a purely somatic growth phase to a stage where it is physiologically capable of reproduction, although social and ecological factors may delay actual breeding. The attainment of sexual maturity in Eleothreptus candicans is relatively rapid compared to some larger caprimulgids, likely an adaptation to the seasonal and unpredictable nature of the cerrado ecosystem, where favorable breeding conditions may be transient. This gonadal maturation is concurrent with the completion of skeleton and plumage development, ensuring that the subadult bird is fully equipped for the demands of territory establishment and courtship displays, which often involve aerial chases and vocalizations that are characteristic of the breeding adult bird.

The onset of actual breeding activity, as distinct from the mere physiological capacity for reproduction, occurs later in the life history of this species. Under the same active metabolic temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], the time since birth at first brood is recorded as approximately 365 days [tR = approximately 365 days]. This indicates that, while a bird may be sexually mature by around two months of age, it typically does not initiate its first nesting attempt until the following breeding season, a delay of roughly one year. This strategy allows the first-year bird to accumulate sufficient lipid and protein reserves, as well as to gain vital experience in foraging and predator avoidance, before investing in the energetically costly process of egg production and incubation. The reproductive output of the species, when it does breed, is characterized by the production of two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], and the female typically completes two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year], a rate that maximizes annual fecundity given the constraints of the brief cerrado wet season. This clutch size is modest, but the double-brooded strategy compensates for high rates of nest predation.

The overall lifespan of the White-winged nightjar, inferred from data on the closely related European nightjar (Caprimulgus europaeus), provides a temporal framework for understanding its reproductive strategy. The maximum recorded longevity for this species under typical environmental conditions, again referenced to a body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], is estimated at 4343.5 days [am = 4343.5 days], which equates to nearly 12 years. This relatively extended lifespan for a bird of this body size allows for several years of reproductive activity, effectively compensating for the low per-clutch output. The life history pattern thus appears to follow a classic slow-fast continuum, where a modest annual fecundity is balanced by high adult survival and repeated breeding opportunities over many seasons. The cerrado habitat, characterized by seasonal fires and fluctuating insect abundance, imposes a selective pressure that favors individuals that can survive multiple breeding attempts rather than investing heavily in a single reproductive event. The senescent adult mortality that eventually ends this reproductive career is likely linked to the gradual deterioration of physiological function and the diminished ability to evade predators or cope with food shortages during lean years.
